label: August 1920
atlas_dek: The episodes of anti-Black violence reported in August 1920 from our dossiers, placed on 1910 county lines and by month (some July events were first reported in August). Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 59 episodes of anti-Black violence reported in August 1920. They come from the 86 located events in the August 1920 table, which includes July events first reported in August. We did not write dossiers for 20 events that were plainly out of scope from the table alone, and 10 more belong to other months or years. Searches covered August papers, plus September papers for more on known episodes.

Four of the 63 dossiers are set aside. Three are duplicates folded into another record: the Ozark report of the Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings lynching in Dale County, Alabama; a San Augustine threat that was a paragraph in the wire story of the Lige Daniels lynching at Center, Texas; and "Rosboro, Oklahoma," a misprint for the Ed Roach lynching at Roxboro, North Carolina. One is out of scope: the Auburndale, Kansas, neighborhood row, a two-sided fight with no injuries.

Police violence is kept generously: beatings in custody, men shot while fleeing or while a warrant was served, and shots fired into a car that did not stop are all included. Only gunfights over a crime in progress are set aside. Where no report gives the victim’s race, the entry says so.

Attacks by one person: our definition covers violence by groups and by people acting with public authority, so an attack by a single private person is normally left out. A later check of every August article for such attacks added seven dossiers: Grover Etheridge’s threats against the Russell Thomas family at Jones Station, Georgia, in June, which drove them to Macon; George Alford’s killing of Ernest Brown near Rome, Georgia; a Houston streetcar conductor who drew a pistol on Gertrude Ford; a white passenger’s threat against a Black passenger on a Beloit train; an assault on a Black minister in Oklahoma City; the ambush killing of Rev. Abe Barner near Eufaula, Oklahoma; and the killing of Henry Golden by an Atlanta streetcar conductor. In all but the Eufaula ambush, where the number of attackers is not stated, the attacker acted alone. If the Houston and Atlanta conductors held police powers, those two are official violence. Whether the rest belong in the count is still open.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched Black and white papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. Black-press clippings are shown as page images and white-press articles as text.

Drafts: no entry has had human review.
